whisper_segs.text: Good morning.
It's 7 o'clock.
It's Monday, March 2nd.
You're welcome to Morning Ireland.
Karen Creed and Audrey Carville with you till 9.
Good morning.
Coming up on the programme, the backlash to President Trump's operation in Iran.
We'll have the latest from the Middle East as the conflict widens with thousands of Irish citizens stranded.
What's the latest advice from the government?
Also, the ongoing travel disruption with flight cancellations.
In business, oil prices jump as markets react to conflict in the Middle East and Bank of Ireland publishes annual results.
And in sport, Shane Lowry denied PGA Tour win while Donegal's footballers and Cork's hurlers continue their unbeaten start to the National Leagues.
We're live on RT Radio 1, the RT Radio app and the news channel.
Your news is read this morning by Karen Carthy.
The conflict in the Middle East has widened.
Overnight, Hezbollah, which is backed by Iran, fired missiles and drones towards northern Israel.
Israel attacked suspected Hezbollah sites in Lebanon.
More than 30 people are reported to have died and almost 150 people have been wounded.
Israeli forces have issued evacuation orders to more than 50 towns and villages across Lebanon.
The UK has given US military forces permission to launch attacks on Iran from UK airfields.
Shortly after the announcement, an RAF base in Cyprus came under drone attack.
The British Prime Minister, Keir Starmer, had initially refused US requests to use RAF bases for strikes on Iran, but announced a change of course last night.
The only way to stop the threat is to destroy the missiles at source.
The United States has requested permission to use British bases for that specific and limited defensive purpose.
Iran has also been launching attacks on Israel and on other Western bases in the region.
The U.S.
Embassy in Kuwait City has come under drone attack with smoke rising from the building.
The joint US-Israeli bombing of Iran is entering its third day.
At the weekend, several Iranian leaders, including Ayatollah,
Ali Khamenei were killed in an airstrike.
There have been waves of further bombardments on areas of the Iranian capital, Tehran.
Last night, the US President Donald Trump returned to Washington from his home in Florida, pledging to avenge the deaths of three US soldiers in the conflict.
Mr Trump said US attacks on Iran would continue until all objectives had been achieved.
Our Washington correspondent, Jackie Fox.
Donald Trump ignored questions on Iran, shouted by reporters as he arrived back at the White House.
It was not long after he released a video statement on social media.
In it, he said the U.S.-Israeli strikes were necessary to eliminate what he called a bloodthirsty terrorist regime armed with nuclear weapons.
President Trump said there will likely be more U.S.
Casualties.
Three U.S.
Service members were killed after Iran struck a base housing American troops in Kuwait.
He also told the New York Times that the assault on Iran could last four to five weeks if necessary.
With concerns being raised on Capitol Hill that the strikes violate congressional authority and lack clear strategic objectives, Congress is set to be briefed by U.S.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio later today.
Jackie Fox, RT News, Washington.
Airlines are continuing to cancel flights across the Middle East.
Dublin Airport has said there's no end in sight to the disruption.
Our Eastern correspondent, Samantha Labrari, reports.
DAA say more than 20 flights were cancelled.
cancelled over the weekend between Dublin and three Middle East airports, Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Doha, which are operated by Etihad, Emirates and Qatar Airways.
Dublin Airport says there's no end in sight to the cancellations, which could continue into the coming days.
DAA says it's working with airlines to assist those impacted.
And while it's a challenge to get through to airline call centres, people should watch online and social platforms and their email for direct contact about cancellations.
Dublin Airport will have extra staff on the ground to provide those affected with help until the issues are resolved.
The Department of Foreign Affairs says there's an estimated 20,000 Irish citizens living and transiting through the region.
Minister Helen McEntee said that no evacuation routes are recommended and that anyone considering taking land routes to neighbouring countries should for now remain sheltered.
Oil prices have increased sharply this morning, rising by 10% at one stage.
Investors are worried that the hostilities in the Middle East will lead to long-term disruption of supply.
Shipping is at a standstill through the Gulf of Hormuz, south of Iran, through which roughly 20% of the world's oil supply has to pass to reach its destination.
And now the weather.
RTE Radio and Weather with Grant.
Future-proof your home and comfort with the HVO Biofuel Ready Grant Vortex Condensing Boiler.
Think heating, think Grant.
Visit grant.ie.
This morning will be dry with sunny spells.
It'll become breezy with scattered showers moving into the west and northwest this morning.
The showers will spread further eastwards this afternoon and evening and become more isolated.
Highest temperatures will range from 8 to 11 degrees.
And there's a warning that south to southwest winds veering northwesterly will reach gale force 8 at times this morning and afternoon on coastal waters from Erishead to Bloody Foreland.
RTE Radio 1 Traffic and Travel with Hyundai.
Celebrating selling more electric cars in January than any other car brand.
At Hyundai dealerships nationwide.
With the latest traffic and travel news, I'm Sinead Ní Uchóin.
There are heavy delays in Dublin on the M50 southbound from Junction 9, Red Cow, to a collision at Junction 12, Firhouse.
It's currently affecting three lanes there.
There's a breakdown also on that motorway, the M50 southbound, between the M1 interchange and Junction 4, Ballymun.
It's in the right lane.
It's slow as well in Dublin heading in on the Nace Road from the M50 to the Longmile Road junction and on the N3 as well towards the city between Junction 4, Clon E and Junction 2, Blanchardstown.
And finally in Cork, there will be a stop-go system on Pope's Road between the Assumption Road and Rathmore Park junctions between 7am and 7pm this week.
And that's the latest traffic and travel news.
Thank you, Sinead.
Here now with It Says in the Papers is John Estoyle.
A terrifying photograph of...
Iran's capital Tehran, with big clouds of smoke rising above it after it was hit in US and Israeli attacks, dominates the front pages of the Irish Times and Irish Independent.
The photograph is by Fatima Bahrami and is run across six columns in the Times.
As the Independent notes, the attacks on Iran killed the leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and 48 members of the top leadership.
As the Times headline sums it up, U.S.
President Trump has thrust the Middle East into a new chapter of uncertainty and chaos.
The paper quotes U.S.
Senator Mark Kelly, a retired combat pilot.
He said, what's the plan for what comes next?
I don't think Donald Trump knows the answer.
Whatever about that, according to a piece in The Independent, Trump thinks he does know how long the conflict with Iran will last.
He's quoted as saying that it could go on for the next four weeks.
It's always been a four-week process.
We figured it will be four weeks or so, he said, not offering any evidence.
The paper says that Iran faces a power vacuum that could leave it in chaos with unforeseeable consequences for the region.
The Times in an editorial describes the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran as a dangerous, illegal and badly conceived military solution to a huge diplomatic and political problem in the Middle East.
The Irish Examiner and Irish Daily Mail lead with reports.
that the US President, speaking to the Atlantic magazine, has said he has agreed to hold talks with Iran's new leadership.
The Irish Sun and Irish Daily Mirror front pages focus on the Irish citizens in the Middle East who have been told by the Department of Foreign Affairs to shelter in place.
The Irish Daily Star leads this morning with a road crash near Ballina County Mayo yesterday in which two teenagers were killed.

In another front page story, the Times reports that Phil Hogan, former Fine Gael minister and European commissioner, is understood to have come through the Department of Agriculture selection process as a potential Irish nominee
to head the Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations.
But Pat Leahy writes that government sources have privately wondered if the state should spend diplomatic and political capital supporting Hogan's candidacy for the post.
He quotes one unnamed source as saying that the Republic doesn't have that many favours to call in right now, especially after opposing the Mercosur trade deal.
Which the European Commission has decided to implement provisionally.
For a breath of air after the news from the Middle East, on the outdoors pages of the Examiner, John G.
O'Dwyer recommends a bracing ramble around the cliff path at Hoth on the north side of Dublin.
The 7.5km moderate walk offers spectacular views.
Tacular views of Dublin Bay and the Irish Sea, he writes.
John, thank you very much.
It's ten past seven.
This is Morning Ireland.
Three days of war with Iran.
The death rate is rising.
Have the latest next.
You're very welcome back to Morning Ireland.
The United States and Israel's war on Iran is entering its third day, with Israel widening its bombing to Lebanon.
The war has decapitated the very top of the Iranian theocratic regime.
Its supreme leader, the Ayatollah, was killed on Saturday.
The head of the all-powerful Revolutionary Guard is dead too, as is the head of the National Defence Council.
In a significant raising of the stakes at home for President Trump, three American service personnel were killed on Sunday.
In a social media message, he defended the war.
Combat operations continue at this time in full force, and they will continue until all of our objectives are achieved.
We have very strong objectives.
They could have done something two weeks ago, but they just couldn't get there.
CENTCOM shared the news that three U.S.
Military service members have been killed in action.
As one nation, we grieve for the true American patriots who have made the ultimate sacrifice for our nation.
Our programme is dominated by this story this morning.
Between now and nine, we will hear from the United States, from Doha.
We'll speak to an Iranian woman living here and get plenty of analysis on the developing situation.
We're going first to Tel Aviv in Israel and we're joined by...
Sukundar Kermani for Foreign Correspondent with Channel 4 News.
Sukundar, thank you very much for joining us once more on Morning Ireland.
Hezbollah has been pulled into this war now and Israel has responded by bombing Lebanon.
What more can you tell us?
Yes, that's right.
This war, as you say, expanding.
I mean, really events unfolding at something of a dizzying pace.
But overnight, Hezbollah launched a number of missile attacks to northern Israel.
Israel responded with heavy airstrikes, including in Beirut.
A number of Lebanese officials had been publicly and privately calling on Hezbollah, of course, an Iranian-backed
militia, not to enter this conflict because of the heavy price Lebanon had paid during the expanded war between
Israel and Hamas and Hezbollah that had been taking place.
Nevertheless, that seems to have happened.
Now we'll see how much further Israel is willing to go in Lebanon.
Some reports suggest that they are planning on striking more Hezbollah targets.
And let's not forget that even after a ceasefire had been agreed between Hezbollah and Israel, that Israel had continued striking on a kind of certainly weekly, if not daily basis, southern Lebanon.
Some other developments overnight.
Iran seems to have successfully hit a...
a major US naval base in Bahrain.
And there have been reports of the US embassy in Kuwait being on fire.
We're awaiting further details on both of those actions.
Meanwhile, in Iran, of course, yet more heavy airstrikes carried out by Israel and the United States.
In relation to those US service personnel who were killed, is there any more detail at all about the circumstances of how that happened?
Not really at this stage.
The suggestion is that they were based in Kuwait.
And separately, we know that a U.S.
Fighter jet pilot ejected after this morning after his plane was crashing.
He, however, seems to have survived.
Of course, this does raise the stakes for Donald Trump.
And it's the first deaths of U.S.
Personnel since this conflict began.
President Trump addressing that, though, in a statement to the American public and warning that there could be further deaths, but that this was something that
the American people would need to take to countenance in order to achieve their aims.
What those aims exactly are seem to be changing.
On the one hand, President Trump yesterday telling some American journalists that he was looking to talk to the new Iranian leadership.
But really quite vague about that.
On the other hand, also telling other American journalists that he's ready to carry
on with this war for many more weeks.
It's very difficult to get independent confirmation of a lot of what is happening in this latest war.
There were reports over the weekend since the strikes began on Saturday of hundreds dying in a school in southern Iran.
Is there any more detail on that, Sukhunder?
Yeah, this was the bloodiest incident that took place or appears to have taken place.
As you say, Iranian state media reporting that more than 100 people were killed in a strike on a girls'school that was full of children on Saturday morning.
So right at the outset of the conflict, this took place in southern Iran.
Now, the school in question is...
According to various OSINT analyses that have been done by independent figures, is right next to an apparent Iranian Revolutionary Guard compound.
So it seems quite possible that that compound was the target.
The school, however, was hit.
And there are video images and testimony from the ground of more than 100 people.
Of course
predominantly schoolgirls being the victims there.
No independent confirmation because Iran restricts access to foreign journalists.
Of course, the Israelis have not commented on that strike.
CENTCOM, the U.S.
Military presence in the region, has said that they're investigating claims of civilian harm.
The Ayatollah, the Supreme Leader, was killed on Saturday.
Who's in charge in Iran now, Sukhinder?
Executive council is currently in charge.
In effect, I think it's really a man called Ali Laranjani, who's one of the few surviving high profile figures in Iran.
Of course, quite possible.
In the coming days by the Israelis and the Americans as well.
Iran had, of course, and the regime had, of course, prepared for this eventuality.
I tell you how many was 86 years old.
So even prior to the conflict, I think everyone knew that.
His death was a matter of time, and certainly with all the noises of the possibility of war, Iran was reported to have developed a succession plan.
Nevertheless, the regime is really sustaining unprecedented blows.
Israeli military officials say that 40 senior commanders in Iran have been killed since the war began.
And at the same time, though, we see that the regime is...
is still intact, is still able to fire at Israel, at Arab Gulf states.
And yesterday we saw large numbers of pro-regime supporters coming out en masse into the streets in Iran to mourn for Ayatollah Khamenei.
That's after the previous night when...
His death was announced and we saw, you know, large groups of young Iranians, particularly coming out onto the streets to celebrate his death.
Of course, he oversaw that brutal, repressive crackdown on Iranian protesters in January, in which thousands of people were killed.
Sukundra, thank you very much indeed.
Sukundra Karmani, foreign correspondent with Channel 4 News live from Tel Aviv.
It's 20 past seven.
Well, the impact of this conflict on air travel continues with widespread disruption.
We have a statement just in from Dublin Airport this morning that all flights scheduled to operate between Dublin Airport and airports in the Middle East today have been cancelled by airlines.
We will have more on this from DAA later in the programme.
But for now, we have been hearing over recent days many Irish who are stranded in the Middle East during this chaos, including 19-year-old Christian Walsh.
He's stuck in Doha with his twin brother, Killian.
On Saturday, they were returning to Dublin from a family holiday in Thailand, where their parents remain.
But when they got to Doha for a connecting flight to Dublin, that was cancelled.
And since then, they've been waiting in a Doha hotel.
Last night, Christian told Keane McCormack he's anxious.
and desperate to get home.
He began by describing to him as he travelled by taxi to his hotel when the flight was cancelled.
When we were going down the motorway, you look to your left and then you see the missiles getting intercepted.
My twin, he was falling asleep because he was knackered.
The taxi man goes to us, there's the missiles being intercepted.
And I was already looking out and I was just in pure shock.
It took me about 35 minutes to actually just...
Come down a bit.
It had me very anxious.
How did you process that?
It was a tough one to process.
I feel like for me, the less I think about it, the better.
So I was just trying to completely forget about it and I just wanted to sleep.
Maybe about 3am, we heard a few missiles being intercepted nearer to the hotel.
What was that like?
I was very stressed at that point.
I thought my world was going to end pretty much.
I'd say I was up for about 30 minutes.
My heart was pounding.
Eventually fell back asleep and then it was over.
How frightened were you when you saw the missiles, when you heard them being intercepted in the hotel?
Oh, I don't think I've ever experienced a Freud like that.
How is your brother?
He's doing well, yeah.
It's great that we have each other.
Definitely, it would be a lot harder if it was just, like, say, one of us.
How are you feeling now?
Because you're still in Doha.
Yep, still in Doha.
No information really.
We're just in the hotel room, chilling out, just trying to forget about it.
We were just watching Ted the movie, just something to laugh at, you know.
Well, the Irish government is warning citizens, Irish citizens already, to shelter in place.
Has the embassy been in contact with you at this stage?
And no, we haven't had any contact with the embassy.
All we've done so far is registered our names down that we are actually in the Gulf States.
Okay, so you registered.
So they know we are there.
What's your biggest hope now?
My biggest hope would be just to be back home soon.
When I heard the bomb, I was only thinking about how precious the word home is, how sacred it is.
All I want is my home.
And that was 19-year-old Christian Walsh from Clondalkin speaking to Keane McCormack from Doha last night.
The government is advising Irish citizens in the Gulf and the wider Middle East region to avoid unnecessary travel and to shelter there following the escalation of the conflict.
There are around 20,000...
1,000 Irish citizens living or transiting through the Middle East and many airports across the region, including in Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Doha, remain closed.

Iranian missiles or drones have hit airports, luxury hotels and other civilian targets across the Gulf, with strikes reported in Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
The Department of Foreign Affairs has set up a consular line that's being manned 24-7 and it is advising people to check the social media platforms for the most up-to-date advice.
Well, for more on Ireland's response to the unrest, we're joined by Thomas Byrne, Minister of State for European Affairs and Defence.
Good morning.
Good morning.
We heard there of that difficult situation Christian and his twin brother are in.
It's not unique.
Many are finding themselves in that situation trying to get home.
What is the latest advice now for them and the many other Irish citizens who are in the region?
Well, my heart goes out to everybody in that situation.
And unfortunately, even on airplane connections, there are hundreds of Irish people affected in that situation.
Hundreds of people on holidays and thousands, as you said, but 15,000 people at least living, for example, in the UAE alone.
So there's huge numbers of Irish people affected.
The advice is to shelter in place.
The airlines at the moment certainly are looking after all of the people who are on connecting flights.
We'll just have to keep ourselves informed of the situation and give the information out as we get it.

be on the department social media platforms and people are encouraged to, obviously as the interviewee there did register on the citizensregistration.dfa.ie website, just so we know exactly who's there.
But we do have an idea, certainly from airlines, as to the numbers of Irish people who are on connecting flights.
In the Gulf and it is quite considerable.
And how many have signed up for this registration platform so far, do we know?
I don't know that figure, but we have general figures as to what we believe the numbers of people in the Gulf are.
And people are signing up all the time.
We definitely encourage them to do that.
And the advice that we are giving to Shelter in Place.
It's the same advice that every EU member state is giving.
Minister McEntee was at the Foreign Affairs Ministers'meeting yesterday online, and the advice is the same across the EU in terms of what their citizens should do.
There's simply nothing else that we can say at the moment, or nothing else that we can recommend at the moment, unfortunately.
Can people be reassured that if they have signed up to this citizens registration platform, that they will be updated immediately if there's any change to the situation so they are aware?
Absolutely.
And that they should also follow the social media platforms of the particularly the UAE embassy.
We've an embassy in Iran, an embassy in Israel, and indeed the Department of Foreign Affairs social media accounts as well.
They'll be posting information as it becomes available and we'll be working with our European colleagues.
to get the best possible information and to have people as safe as possible.
And in contact with colleagues in the Gulf countries, but also as well in the airlines as well.
We are in contact with people.
There are plenty of Irish people, as it happens, working for some of these major airlines.
And I think that there's good information coming about the Irish people over there.
As we heard there, people are worried, they're distressed and some will be considering all options.
And there are land routes to neighbouring countries such as Oman, but the advice is not to pursue anything other than a shelter that's in place.
That's the strategy for now.
That's been clear.
If the evacuation was needed, what plans are in place?
What is the Irish government preparing for?
Look, we're looking at all possible eventualities, but the simple reality is we can't recommend those land routes because of the sheer numbers of Irish people that are there.
If one or two people do them, and it may well be you'll see people on the radio or television who've succeeded in doing this today, but the reality is we can't recommend this.
For over 10,000 people because we simply don't know what the consequences could be.
It does not appear to us to be safe.
You may get to another country, but the question would be, would you be able to fly out of that country?
So it's not something that we can recommend.
And that's why the advice very clearly has to be to shelter in place.
And as things develop, we're continuing to examine the situation, see what the options might be for people who want to leave.
And that will be done in close coordination with all of our EU allies.
I think that it is very, very important that we're in the European Union.
We know what's going on and we can get...
operation if it's necessary, but for the moment, that advice stays the same to shelter in place.
And European ministers have met virtually on this unrest.
EU governments, including Ireland, have also been largely cautious in their response around the US and Israeli military attack, expressing concern with calls for de-escalation.
It is, though, in contrast to opposition politicians who say what happened was illegal under international law.
Why is there no condemnation by the Irish government?
Well, look, my main priority is the Irish citizens who are abroad and who are worried sick about what's going to happen.
I think that has to be our first concern.
There'll be time for all of that subsequently.
The fact of the matter is that there is a conflict developing.
There are missiles going into tourism areas at the moment, certainly yesterday.
And we have to be concerned about the Irish citizens there.
That's my focus.
The British didn't, for example, did not take part in the initial strikes, but now feel that they have a legal right to do what they're doing in terms of lending some of their basis to the US
because of British citizens being attacked and British installations being targeted.
So this is a highly complex and evolving situation.
And the Irish government has to take the interests of Irish citizens first.
And with the interests of Irish citizens, and the United Nations Charter Minister has been outlined on many occasions in light of this attack, saying that
two justifications can happen in self-defence in the face of an imminent threat and approval by the UN, and neither there's thought.
And so it...
Does beg the question, does Ireland feel constrained from criticising a key ally like the US?
I wouldn't say that at all.
I mean, it's certainly a fact that this is not an invitation by the UN Security Council.
That's a fact.
But as regards to the legal position, the legal justification, that's for those who are involved in it to justify at this particular moment until a further determination can be made.
But our priority has to be the many, many Irish citizens and many of them will be listening to this programme to look for some glimmer of hope, some glimmer of advice.
And as I said, the advice, unfortunately, for the moment has to be to shelter in place.

But almost all the resources available to the Department of Foreign Affairs today will be answering calls from citizens and engaging with European colleagues all around the European Union and indeed with colleagues in the Gulf.
To assess the updated situation and keep those citizens at the forefront of our minds.

And just briefly, because we are hearing of this conflict widening overnight, if there is the situation where evacuations are needed, can we get help from our European allies, considering that there's around 20,000 Irish currently in that region?
Well, look, there are a huge number of Irish, huge numbers of Irish, half and all expressed a desire to leave, because many of them are there for quite some time.
We've Irish people in Iran, small numbers in Israel.
And of course, we have our soldiers in Lebanon as well, where there has been some incidents last night as well, this morning.
The information I have is that all of our soldiers are safe and there's no cause for concern there at the moment.
but we're always concerned about them.
But I think, yes, we will be able to work with our European allies if evacuations could be done and if they should be done.
But all that work would go on.
And I mean, this is at a very, very early stage.
I mean, it started to happen just at the weekend and everybody's assessing what's safe, what's not safe and how do we best protect our citizens.
OK, Thomas Byrne, Minister of State for European Affairs and Defence, thanks very much for speaking to us.
It is just after half past seven and we'll get the news headlines with Karen.

Iran has also been launching attacks on Israel and other Western bases in the region.
The US embassy in...
has come under drone attack, with smoke seen rising from the building.

motor finance business.

Looking for his first win on tour as an individual since 2022.

And I think shades of Dubai in January when he lost out in similar circumstances.

I'm obviously extremely disappointed.
I had the tournament in my hands and I threw it away.

But, yeah, look.
What can I say?
I played unbelievable all day and then won by a shot in 16 and completed me through me for the last three holes.

Couldn't feel the club face in the last three holes then after my tee shot in 16.
It was strange.
You know, what can I say?
It's very, very disappointing.
Jeez, like, this is going to be hard to take, yeah.
Dubai was hard at the start of the year, but this is going to be pretty hard, yeah.
Yeah, I think it's going to take him a while to get over that one.
Indeed, he sounds quite shocked as well to me.

So tune into that after the news at 8.30.

Four in Qatar, yeah, and we were previously in Bahrain for six years.
It's been quite intense at times.
We've seen lots of projectiles flying across the sky and being intercepted.
Are you concerned?
I wouldn't be telling you the truth if I said I wasn't concerned.

Qatar have done a fantastic job of keeping everybody up to date, keeping everybody safe with the shelter in place and their efforts to deter and destroy anything that's coming in.
You're not planning on moving any time soon, by the sounds of it.
You're pretty confident with the efforts that are being made.
Yeah, yeah, like this is a very extraordinary situation and on the day-to-day norm, the Middle East is a very safe place to be.

Adam Maguire from our business desk has been looking at this this morning.
So oil prices first, Adam, what's happening there?
Yeah, they're up sharply this morning, Audrey.
Initially this morning in the early hours, they rose by about 10%.
They cooled off slightly.
Now looking like they could break through that 10% barrier once again.
Barrel of Brent crude currently around 9.4% higher.
Barrel of West Texas intermediate up 8.8%.
Now that's down to concerns around production and distribution of oil and gas.
Iran itself, of course, an oil producing nation, as well as some of the neighbouring countries that have been targeted by attacks.

because over the weekend, Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, which last year facilitated around 20% of global oil and gas shipments.

Maybe soon be seen at the petrol stations?
Potentially.

Yeah, but obviously, and then it's a case of whether it holds at the current higher rate or whether it maybe falls back if things settle down a bit.

Higher oil prices, of course, mean higher costs for them.

Iran specifically targeting regional airports in its retaliatory attacks, which is impacting flights.

Air France KLM shares down 7.3%.
